title: Modify Authentication Process: Password Filter DLL
shortTitle: Modify Authentication Process: Password Filter DLL
summary: Windows password filters are dynamic libraries that the Local Security Authority loads in order to enforce password policy before a new password is accepted into the Security Accounts Manager. Because a filter must judge the candidate password itself, the operating system hands it the real plaintext value during every password set or reset. An adversary can register a malicious filter by placing a library on the host and adding its name to the notification packages value in the registry, after which that library receives every password submitted on the machine or, if installed on a domain controller, across the whole domain. The library can approve the change as required and simultaneously write the account name and password to a hidden file or send them elsewhere. Artefacts include new library files in system directories, edits to the notification packages registry value, and writes from the authentication process to unusual paths. Genuine filters are few and well known, so an unexpected entry is suspicious, but compliance products do install filters, which is why a change record, file hash and signature matter.

beginner.definition: A password filter is a small program that checks new passwords on Windows. It sees the password in plain text so that it can judge whether the password is strong enough. This technique means an attacker installs a fake filter that copies every new password.
beginner.whyItMatters: Passwords pass through this check in a readable form, so a fake filter sees all of them. The stolen passwords are real and current, which makes them immediately useful to an attacker. A filter placed on a domain controller collects passwords for the whole domain. Because the filter must approve each change, the system keeps working and nobody complains.
howItWorks: When you set a new Windows password, the system asks each registered filter to approve it.
To judge the password, the filter needs the plain text value and not a hash.
An attacker signs up their own library as a filter using a registry setting.
From then on, every password change is passed to that library in clear text.
The library approves the password as required and quietly saves a copy somewhere else.
If installed on a domain controller, it captures password changes for the whole domain.
beginner.example: Imagine a company where every new employee's identity form must be checked by a small team. The team confirms the form and stamps it approved. Now somebody joins that team with a hidden photocopier beside the desk. Every form still gets stamped, so the process looks completely normal from outside. But the newcomer quietly copies each form and keeps the copies in a drawer. Nobody notices anything, because the approval still happens quickly and correctly.
takeaways: A password filter receives plaintext passwords by design, so it must be trustworthy.
Review the registry list of registered password filters and the files they point to.
Any unexpected filter on a domain controller should be treated as a serious incident.

objectives: Explain what a Windows password filter does and why it needs plaintext passwords.
Describe how a malicious filter is registered and what information it collects.
Identify the registry and file system evidence of an added filter.
Explain the difference in impact between a local filter and one on a domain controller.
Compare genuine policy filters with unauthorised additions.
